title: Morphology of Flowering Plants
tagline: Roots, stems and leaves: forms, modifications and functions; inflorescence; flower, fruit and seed structure and terminology.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Biology registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Morphology is the study of the external form of plants. In flowering plants, the body is built from a few basic organs: roots, stems, leaves and flowers, each of which can take very different forms depending on the life of the plant. A root may store food, a stem may climb or store water, a leaf may catch insects, and a flower may be arranged singly or in a cluster. In this chapter we learn the standard parts and terminology, and then see how the same organs can be modified for storage, support, climbing, protection and reproduction.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Root, stem and leaf forms and modifications; flower structure and terms; inflorescence; fruit and seed; semi-technical description and floral formula/diagram

learningOutcomes: Describe the main parts of a flowering plant and their functions.
Distinguish tap, fibrous and adventitious roots.
Classify root and stem modifications by function.
Differentiate simple and compound leaves and recognise venation and phyllotaxy.
Recognise the parts of a flower and use basic floral terminology.

blocks.text: The root is usually the underground part of the plant, but not always. A tap root grows from the radicle and is the main root in many dicots. A fibrous root system has many roots of similar size, common in monocots. Adventitious roots arise from parts other than the radicle, such as stems or leaves. Roots may also be modified for special functions: some store food, some help the plant breathe in waterlogged soil, and some give extra support.

items: Tap root is the main root from the radicle.
Fibrous root system has many roots of similar size.
Adventitious roots arise from non-root parts.
Root modifications include storage, respiration and support.

items.text: A carrot is a tap root modified for storage. In some plants growing in marshy soil, roots grow upward to get air, which is an adaptation to waterlogged conditions.
items.note: The root’s shape alone does not tell you its function; the plant’s habitat and the structure’s details matter too.

blocks.text: The stem bears branches, leaves and flowers and contains the nodes and internodes. Stems may be herbs, shrubs or trees depending on their strength and lifespan. They can also be modified. Underground stems store food and help the plant survive unfavourable seasons. Some stems climb, and some are reduced to thorns for protection. A useful test is to look for buds and scale leaves at the nodes, because those are stem features even when the stem is highly modified.

items: A stem has nodes and internodes.
Stems can be herbs, shrubs or trees.
Underground stems include structures such as rhizomes, corms and tubers.
Stems may climb or be modified into thorns.
Buds and scale leaves are stem clues, even in modified stems.

items.text: A potato tuber is a modified stem because it has ‘eyes’, which are buds at the nodes. A carrot, by contrast, is a root and does not have these bud-bearing nodes.
items.note: The presence of buds is one of the clearest ways to tell a stem modification from a root modification.

learn.title: Leaf: parts, venation, types and modifications

blocks.text: A typical leaf has a leaf base, a petiole and a lamina. The lamina may have a midrib and veins, and the pattern of veins is the venation. Leaves may be simple or compound. Their arrangement on the stem is phyllotaxy. Leaves can also be modified: some become tendrils for climbing, some become spines for protection, and some are adapted for storage or insect capture. Classification matters here because the same organ can serve very different purposes.

items: A leaf has leaf base, petiole and lamina.
Venation may be reticulate or parallel.
Leaves may be simple or compound.
Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on the stem.
Leaf modifications include tendrils, spines, storage leaves and insectivorous leaves.

items.text: In a compound leaf, the lamina is divided into leaflets, while in a simple leaf the lamina is entire or only shallowly incised but not truly divided into leaflets. This distinction is important when identifying leaf types.
items.note: Compound and simple leaves can look similar at a glance, so the presence of a true leaf base and bud at the node helps identify the leaf there.

blocks.text: The flower is the reproductive structure of a flowering plant. Flowers may appear singly or in clusters on the floral axis. The arrangement of flowers on the axis is the inflorescence. In racemose inflorescences, the main axis continues growing and flowers develop in a definite order. In cymose inflorescences, the main axis ends in a flower and growth continues from lateral branches. A flower itself has whorls such as calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium, and it can be described using terms for symmetry, completeness and the way parts are fused or attached.

items: A flower may be solitary or arranged in an inflorescence.
Inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.
Racemose: main axis continues; flowers in acropetal order.
Cymose: main axis ends in a flower; growth comes from lateral branches.
Flower parts include calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.

items.text: A raceme and a cyme can both look like clusters of flowers, but they differ in whether the main axis keeps growing and in the order in which flowers open.
items.note: Inflorescence type is about arrangement and development, not just how many flowers are present.

blocks.text: A fruit develops from the ovary after fertilisation and contains the seed or seeds. The fruit may be fleshy or dry, and it may open to release seeds or remain closed. A seed is the mature ovule and contains the embryo and food reserves. Describing fruits and seeds uses a set of standard terms, and being able to recognise the fruit parts helps in identifying plants and understanding their reproduction.

items: A fruit develops from the ovary after fertilisation.
Fruits may be fleshy or dry.
A seed contains the embryo and food reserves.
Fruit and seed structures are used in plant description and identification.

items.text: A mango fruit is fleshy and develops from a single ovary, while a pea pod is a dry fruit that splits open at maturity.
items.note: The difference is not just texture; it reflects different fruit types and different ways of releasing seeds.

keyPoints: Morphology describes the external form and its relation to function.
Roots may be tap, fibrous or adventitious, and may be modified for storage, respiration or support.
Stems have nodes and internodes and may be modified into underground, climbing or protective forms.
Buds at nodes help distinguish stem modifications from root modifications.
Leaves have leaf base, petiole and lamina; venation, simple/compound form and phyllotaxy matter.
Flowers may be solitary or arranged in racemose or cymose inflorescences.
examFocus: When asked to distinguish a root from a stem modification, look for buds or scale leaves at nodes and for the plant part from which the structure arises.
Do not confuse a flower with an inflorescence; the inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the axis.

vocabulary.meaning: The study of the external form and structure of an organism.
The main root developing from the radicle, with lateral roots branching from it.
A root arising from a part of the plant other than the radicle.
The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.
The arrangement of leaves on the stem.
A change in form of a plant organ to suit a particular function.

questions.prompt: A root arising from a part of the plant other than the radicle is called:
questions.explanation: Adventitious roots arise from parts other than the radicle, such as stems or leaves.
questions.commonMistake: Calling every lateral root adventitious without checking where it arises.

questions.prompt: Which feature is a strong clue that an underground storage structure is a stem rather than a root?
questions.explanation: Buds at nodes are stem features; their presence suggests a stem modification rather than a root.
questions.commonMistake: Using storage or thickness alone, which roots can also have.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between racemose and cymose inflorescence.
questions.answer: In racemose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow and flowers develop in acropetal order. In cymose inflorescence, the main axis ends in a flower and further growth comes from lateral branches.
questions.explanation: The key difference is whether the main axis keeps growing and how the flowers are arranged during development.
questions.commonMistake: Saying one is ‘more advanced’ without describing the order of development.

questions.prompt: Why is a potato tuber considered a stem modification?
questions.answer: Because it bears buds at its nodes, and buds and scale leaves are stem features.
questions.explanation: The presence of buds at nodes is the classic clue that a tuber is a modified stem, not a root.
questions.commonMistake: Saying it is a stem only because it stores food, which roots also do.

questions.prompt: Compare carrot and potato as storage organs on the basis of the plant part involved and the features that support your answer.
questions.answer: A carrot is a tap root modified for storage, so it lacks the bud-bearing nodes of a stem. A potato tuber is a modified stem and has buds at its nodes, which are stem features. The presence of these buds is the main evidence that the potato is a stem.
questions.explanation: The comparison should identify the organ in each case and give the structural features that support that identification.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the two because both store food, without mentioning buds or the organ of origin.
